b: State: discussion Scope: what a Linux guest needs from the emulator's Windows host. A Linux guest runs on the Windows host once four system calls answer as they do on Linux. A Rust guest linked against static glibc failed on the Windows host, translated and interpreted alike, and so did the released addon. The first three fixes left the crash in place. The emulator's Windows host answers four system calls as its Linux host does: - brk keeps the new break. - clock_gettime writes the 64-bit guest's two 64-bit fields. - Error numbers map to the Linux numbers in one header. - sched_getaffinity reports one CPU, as the Linux and macOS hosts do. Check that the Windows host answers brk , clock_gettime , error numbers and sched_getaffinity as the Linux host does. What went wrong The emulator's Windows host answered four system calls differently from its Linux host: - brk did not keep the new break. Static glibc puts the main thread's thread-local block at the first break, so the heap handed out memory inside it and, later, an address in read-only data. This was the crash. - clock_gettime wrote the host's own timespec , a 32-bit nanosecond field with padding, where the 64-bit guest reads two 64-bit fields. - Error numbers above ERANGE follow the Windows C runtime ( ENOSYS is 40, where Linux has 38). glibc chooses its rseq and clone3 fallbacks on ENOSYS , so the host now maps errors to the Linux numbers in one header. - sched_getaffinity was missing. The Linux and macOS hosts report one CPU, and the Windows host now does the same. How the break was found A dump of the guest registers and the page's permissions at the fault found the break. The fixes are in our libriscv fork, and the addon takes them with Linux's ENOSYS for an unknown system call. b: State: discussion Scope: the timed garment handover, its legs, its load and its checks. The garment handover is timed leg by leg, so a slow leg shows up where it happens. The round trip from a player's desk to the store's region measured 22 to 28 ms. Which leg of the handover spends it? The store and the backend stay together in one region, and the zones run on a server near the players (operator, 2026-10-23). The handover is the step that crosses the round trip, and the rung times it. The measure is per server and per leg, never a count of servers to minimise (operator, 2026-10-23). The time runs from the worker zone finishing the garment to its ghost drawn in the players' zone, split by leg: the store commit, the ownership handover, and the fetch by hash. The load is a replay of recorded pen strokes with the players' recorded head and hand tracks, pauses included, never scripted motion. It holds for 5 minutes and is judged on the 95th and 99th percentiles, never on a mean. Run the timed handover: replay the recorded pen strokes for 5 minutes and read the 95th and 99th percentiles of each leg. Why several servers Running several servers is expected: a system that tolerates faulty or lying members needs more machines to match one machine's reliability, so the measure is per server and per leg. Rules of the run - A zone confirms a handover only after the store commits it. Writes may group into one commit, and every waiter waits for that commit. - The zone's tick never waits on the store. - A player who pauses keeps their session. The replay's pauses must not cause a reconnect. - The report names what stopped the run: tick time, memory, the store commit, or sessions. - The first run on a new host repeats a reference build, so a change of machine is not read as a change of code. Checks and controls Checks, each with a control that must fail: - The legs add up to the measured total. A control that adds a delay to the store commit must show up in that leg and nowhere else. - No player sees a garment confirmed before its commit. A control that confirms first must be caught. - The replay is not the bottleneck: the replay host's own load is reported beside the zone's, and a control that throttles the replay must be named as the limit. Pass limits The pass limits are not set yet: the first sustained run measures them, and the operator sets them from it. b: State: discussion Feature: a garment that crosses itself starts the cloth-fit solve as one clean surface. Scope: the proxy garment that the cloth-fit solve fits, and how its result returns. Can a garment that crosses itself start the cloth-fit solve clean? The pants cross themselves 1316 times across 53 shells. The solver takes one connected manifold mesh with no crossings, and a union of those shells did not give one. A surface of the garment's distance field might. - The garment is repaired as a proxy. The original keeps its UVs, skin weights and materials. - The proxy is a level surface of the unsigned distance to the garment. Open edges close and layers closer than the distance merge (operator, 2026-11-01). - The proxy takes skin weights from the garment through the robust weight transfer guest. The fitted displacement returns to the original through the cage stage. - The repair uses no CoACD hulls and no CSG union of the shells (operator, 2026-11-01). Count the crossing pairs and the shells of the proxy. The solve takes it when they read 0 and 1, and a planted second shell must read 2. What the solver takes The cloth-fit solver's input spec asks for an avatar of one or more closed surfaces, because the avatar becomes a signed distance field. It asks for a garment that is a connected manifold triangle mesh. The solver also refuses a start where the garment crosses itself. The solver's own example solves. Its garment is one shell with no non-manifold edge, 144 open edges (a hem and a waist) and 0 crossing pairs. Its avatar is 32 shells that cross each other 1394 times between shells. So the body may overlap itself, and the garment may not. What an outfit piece looks like Measured with a throwaway script that welds at one hundred-thousandth of the bounding box and tests each edge against each triangle that shares no vertex. A planted crossing reads 1 and a planted separate pair reads 0. - The pants have 53 shells, no non-manifold edge, 399 open edges and 1316 crossing pairs. Of those, 1300 are between shells and 16 are inside one shell. - The skirt has 43 shells and 12 open loops. - The kimono has 346 shells, 128 open loops and 77 non-manifold edges. - The pants have 982 vertices that sit twice at one position, and no triangle collapses. What did not work A union of the shells did not give a clean surface. Each shell became a solid: an inner copy offset along the vertex normals, joined to the shell by a strip on every open edge. A stock CSG union then ran on all 53 solids. - At 4 mm, about five credit cards stacked, 24 of the 53 solids came out inside out, because the small shells are thinner than the offset. - At 1 mm, about one credit card, all solids were valid. The union still had 295 non-manifold edges and 30969 crossing pairs, against 1316 before. Convex hulls from CoACD are closed and cover the garment, but the operator ruled them out for the repair. The pants gave 9 hulls in 6 seconds. The distance field MuJoCo's mesh compiler builds an octree of signed distances. It finds the closest triangle through a bounding-volume hierarchy. It takes the sign from the angle-weighted pseudonormal of the closest vertex, edge or face, so it casts no rays and counts no windings. MuJoCo's GPU port only evaluates that field. The proxy uses the unsigned distance, so the sign never decides the surface. A level surface of it wraps every open edge and cannot cross itself. The distance is an argument that the operator picks. The solver's contact distance is 2 mm, about three credit cards stacked. Rigging and carrying back The robust weight transfer guest takes the garment as source and the proxy as target. Its arrays are bone-major. It builds its Laplacian with intrinsic mollification (operator, 2026-11-01). With two vertices at one position, a plain cotangent Laplacian gave non-finite weights for 480 of 484 outputs on a test grid, and the mollified one stayed finite. The cage stage binds the original to a cage and moves it with the fitted proxy. That gives a smooth field. Copying the nearest vertex's displacement does not. What is not known - Whether a level surface at the contact distance keeps the garment's folds. - Whether it is one shell. The first step counts shells on the pants. - Whether the solver takes a garment of several shells. That needs the solver build on the Windows desk. - Whether the garments wind consistently. The unsigned field does not need it. - Where the nearest-triangle query runs as a guest, and its speed on a 54000-vertex piece. Related - RFD66606-2424, where a sketch is placed on the avatar before any fit. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2435: a garment is repaired as a distance-field surface

b: State: discussion Feature: two people in one campus zone see each other's avatars from a program that runs alone. Scope: the see-each-other beta feature as its own native program, its gate and its control. Can two people see each other from a program that needs nothing else in the beta? The beta lists seeing each other first, and nothing built yet carries it alone. A slice that needs voice, the pen and the adventure party to run depends on all three. - Presence ships as one native program with no editor or browser. It owns the zone's list of people and their avatar poses (operator, 2026-11-01). - The slice runs with no voice, pen, adventure party or shop present. Its inputs are recorded pose streams in place of those parts (operator, 2026-11-01). - Native means a riscv64 guest ELF for the sandbox, run binary-translated (operator, 2026-11-01). Its gates run on the CPU guest as the parity oracle (RFD66606-2374, RFD66606-2390). - The host is the win64 build of RFD66606-2360, built natively for the Steam Frame and the Steam Deck, and the slice's gates run there too (operator, 2026-11-12). Run the sight gate against a recorded pose stream. A zone that drops one side's poses must fail it. What the beta asks The beta's first feature is two people in the campus zone, one in the standalone Steam Frame and one on the desktop. Each sees the other's avatar. The slice holds that and nothing more: who is in the zone, where each avatar stands, and the pose each person sends. The campus A campus is a world, and a world runs as instances. Any player starts an instance for friends, public or invite-only. One zone server is the authority for one instance. Each instance keeps its own shop books. One campus ships first, and building a campus stays with the V-Sekai content tools (operator, 2026-10-30). The slice's edge In: the zone's list of people, a pose from each, and a view of the others for each person. Out: voice, outfits, seats and books, which are the sibling slices. The edge is a message shape between the zone and a client. It is the only contract the slice shares, and its first step writes it down. Gates and controls Each gate has a control that plants the defect and must fail. - Sight: two clients replay a pose stream, and each client's view lists the other's avatar at the replayed pose. Control: a zone that drops one client's poses. - Alone: the program starts and passes its sight gate with every sibling slice absent. Control: a sibling's message planted in the input, which the program must refuse by name. Frontier learning picks the runs The slice's gates run as levels in RFD66606-2309's sense, scheduled the way RFD66606-2323 schedules the store's attacks. A level is an input family with fixed attributes: the number of people in the zone, the pose rate, the client side (stream or desktop), and the loss pattern in the recorded pose stream. A problem is one 5 minute replay of a pose stream with a drawn seed and offset. Level Planted defect Found when pose drop the zone drops one client's poses a client's view misses the other avatar pose order the zone swaps two poses an avatar seen at an older pose than the replay self echo the zone lists a person to themselves a view that lists its own avatar late join the zone skips the list for a late client a late client sees nobody sibling input a sibling's message planted the program accepts it Each level runs on the slice as it is and on the slice with that level's defect planted. On the planted target, success is the defect found. Regret 1[s ≥ 1] − s/n over the last eight runs is high when a level finds its defect only some of the time. Mutation moves one attribute and is kept only when the planted find rate rises. A clean run counts only after its level found the planted defect in each of its last eight runs. A finding on the real slice is never averaged into a rate: it stops the lane and becomes a level that runs every time. The runs are guest ELF runs on the CPU guest, which is the parity oracle, so no gate here needs a GPU. Where the code lands Each slice is a repository of its own in our organization, named for what it does with no game name, and pinned through the repo manifest. It arrives as an ordinary pull request. V-Sekai repositories stay read-only. What is not known - Which pose message shape the standalone Frame client and the desktop client both send. The first step reads it from the clients and writes it down. - Whether a zone holds the pose rate for two people. Nothing has run, and no number is claimed. The problem RFD66606-2360 lists four features and names no way to build one without the others. The tuples rebac rfd-2436--provides--see-each-other rfd-2436--spends--binary-translated-only-timings rfd-2436--spends--elf-guest-native-translation rfd-2436--is-a--native-slice Related - RFD66606-2360, the one beta. - The sibling slices, RFD66606-2437 to RFD66606-2440, are abandoned (operator, 2026-11-11). b: State: committed Feature: a 64 Hz 3D state server is judged by tick-to-send time at a held user count. Scope: the metric, budget, sweep and pass rule for the entity server on one droplet. How many users can one shared vCPU serve at 64 Hz before a tick runs late, and what would show it? A feed server that holds 295,000 readers at a p99 of 117 ms spends about seven and a half ticks on its tail. It serves reads, so neither its user count nor its latency says anything about a tick. The user count is whatever 64 Hz allows. Latency is the metric (operator, 2026-11-07). - The tick is fixed at 64 Hz, 15,625,000 ns. - The primary figure is server-side tick-to-send time, from packet received to batched datagram handed to the kernel, at p50, p95 and p99. The proposed budget is p99 under 4 ms, a quarter of a tick. - Tick overruns, missed deadlines and steal time from the host's CPU counters are recorded beside it, so a hypervisor stall is attributed and not blamed on the code. - The rule is pass or fail, not rank. Raise users in a sweep to the knee where p99 crosses the budget. A run passes with 0% errors over a 5 minute hold. - Only bytes derived from the code are stated, and no network figure is measured. - A figure stays labelled derived until a measured one replaces it. The first gate: a load generator holds a fixed user count for 5 minutes and prints server-side tick-to-send p50, p95 and p99, and a planted slow handler pushes p99 over budget and fails the run. The problem The only public reference is a read-heavy feed benchmark that reports users held and request rate. Neither says whether a 15.625 ms tick completes in time. Derived figures All of these are arithmetic on the reference cost of 26 microseconds per operation, not measurements. - Operations per second are 128 times the user count: 64 inbound and 64 batched outbound per user. - One core at 100% does 38,461 operations per second. At 128 users that is 16,384, about 42.6% busy. At 150 users it is 49.9%, the floor with tail headroom. At 300 users it is 99.8%. - The 26 microseconds include HTTP parsing and SQLite reads, which the tick path drops. Bytes - An entity packet is 100 bytes, so inbound is 6,400 bytes per second per user. - Twelve entities in view make 1,200 bytes of data and 1,248 bytes with IP and UDP headers, under the 1,280 byte IPv6 minimum. Sixteen make 1,600 bytes and fragment, so more datagrams split them. - Outbound is users times entities times 6,400. At 128 users and 12 entities that is 9,830,400 bytes per second, about 25.5 TB in 30 days. The droplet's transfer allowance is not verified, so egress may bind before the CPU, and the entities in view are the main lever. Steal time A shared vCPU can lose a few milliseconds to the hypervisor, a large share of a tick. Whether the droplet is one shared vCPU is assumed and not verified. Related - RFD66606-2443, the server that this metric judges. - The droplet here is the benchmark host. Where the ghost servers run is open: Fly is a non-goal (RFD66606-2490, operator, 2026-11-12). - Gate evidence: the feed server, CI run 42417791013, job tick-budget (success). It proves a p99 under 4 ms budget on a 64-tick loopback check. The 5-minute hold at fixed user counts and the sweep to the knee are not run yet, so the gate is unproven. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2442: latency is the metric for 64 Hz entity state

b: State: committed Feature: a sibling EntityServer serves 64 Hz 3D state beside FeedServer. Scope: the transport repository: entity modules, one executable, the codec, the load generator. Can the feed server's ring, store and layers carry a tick loop without a second copy of any of them? The repository already has the io_uring glue with a provided-buffer ring, a store that opens FoundationDB through a VFS, and layered proofs. It has no tick, no packet codec and no load generator. EntityServer is a sibling of FeedServer in the same repository, built by the same lakefile (operator, 2026-11-07). It reuses the ring glue, the JWT layer and the store, and edits them where they must change. It adds no parallel copy. - State lives in memory in a flat array. The tick path does no SQLite and no disk I/O. - The 100 byte packet layout has one source, the entity packet contract, taken by subtree. EntityServer never re-emits the offsets. - The tick kernel is written in a restricted Lean subset with proofs and emitted as standalone C99 with fixed-capacity arrays and no heap. The ring loop stays hand-written C. - Pose goes by datagram. Join, leave and ownership go on a small reliable channel. - The timer uses absolute deadlines on the monotonic clock. An overrun coalesces or drops, and never queues a backlog. - Each client owns its own avatar entity, so pose has no write conflicts. Store writes happen behind the tick. The first gate: a binary ticks at 64 Hz on Linux, sends a fixed batch of 12 entities to one registered address, and prints tick-to-send percentiles. The problem The repository's own record was partly stale. The store path through FoundationDB, its header and the subtree are on the main branch. Parity and profile figures in the divergence notes were measured on SQLite, not on FoundationDB, and the README said the submission has no FoundationDB code. Rungs - Skateboard: timer, UDP socket, fixed batch of 12 entities, tick-to-send percentiles printed. - Multishot receive into the existing buffer ring, and a session table keyed by address. - The codec from the contract, with two proofs: a decode reads no more than 100 bytes, and a batch with headers stays within 1,280 bytes. - Area-of-interest grid, so fan-out is users times entities in view, not users squared. - Load generator and sweep, with a control that fails: a planted slow handler that pushes p99 over budget. - Write-behind to the node's store, then two nodes. Acceptance - The emitted C builds with strict C99 warnings as errors, and the tick object has no allocation or runtime symbols. - Fixtures through the Lean semantics and through the emitted C give identical bytes, and a planted bug in the C makes that check fail. - The tick kernel has zero unproved goals. No MISRA conformance is claimed. - The default feed path keeps passing its diff and smoke scripts. - On the CPU runner, only checks that need no cluster run. A live FoundationDB check is an integration test. Open Extend the in-house emitter, which emits only the codec header today, or vendor the Trust-Lean compiler by subtree. One source either way, never a copy or a submodule. - Gate evidence: the feed server, CI run 42417791013, jobs tick-budget and client sweeps (success). entity_serve.c fails a run whose p99 is over 4 ms, and the planted-defect sweeps are caught. The Lean tick kernel and its emitted-C byte check are not in the repo, so the Lean-to-C acceptance is unmet and stated as such. Related - RFD66606-2442, the latency metric that judges this server. - RFD66606-2044, Lean at build time and a flat C ABI at run time. - RFD66606-2304, the one Lean library that generates a C planner through the same compiler. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2443: EntityServer serves 64 Hz entity state beside FeedServer

b: State: discussion Feature: a record of five checks a security pass never ran, so the pass is not called finished. Scope: the MCP-to-A2A bridge server, and the Godot editor's MCP listener and its new A2A route. Can a security pass call itself finished while five of its own claims stay unchecked? Eight pull requests closed a prompt-injection finding, moved a bridge server and an editor listener to the Agent2Agent protocol's 1.0 wire format, and closed a browser-origin hole in both of the listener's protocols. Every pull request carries tests that passed on one machine. Five verification gaps stay open, and work on them does not resume until this record changes. - No diff against the operator's own A2A listener script, which was never recovered. - No run on the Windows desk or inside the resident editor session the operator described. - No run against the Agent2Agent protocol's conformance suite, for either system. - No real browser has exercised the new Origin refusal, only a forged command-line header. - Both systems' test commands still force a hidden display, against the windowed-test rule. Read the five gaps below before picking any of this work back up, and close one gap at a time. The five gaps, and what closes each one - Godot parity. The operator ran a resident editor with an uncommitted listener script added to its MCP addon, serving A2A at one address with a card and two commands. That script was never pushed anywhere and could not be found on any branch, so the listener that shipped is a clean-room build from the protocol specification, not a check against the original. Closes when that original script is pushed to a branch and the two are diffed line by line. - The Windows desk. Every check so far ran on a Mac, in a real window, never headless. Closes when the same checks run once on the desk, inside the resident editor session. - A conformance suite. Both systems were checked against the official client library and against each other, never against the protocol's own conformance suite. Closes when that suite is identified by name and run once against each system, with its own report kept. - A real browser. The Origin refusal was proven with a command-line client sending a forged header, never with a browser tab. Closes when an actual browser page, opened by a person, is shown the refusal. - The hidden-display test commands. Both systems' committed test commands still pass a flag that hides the window, against the rule that a Godot test runs where it can be watched. Every check in this pass ran windowed by hand instead, by overriding the command each time. Closes when the committed command itself drops the flag and still passes. Related - No earlier RFD names either system; this is their first register entry. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2446: A2A hardening leaves five verification gaps open

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the navigator should show each RFD's earliest and latest possible time and route. Scope: the generator here, and the navigator and its planner in the persona repository. Can the navigator show a temporal route and state durations for the beta's RFDs when no RFD states a duration yet? The navigator plans the beta's route from the RFDs' own token edges, a cone of 33 RFDs and 37 steps. The persona planner now produces temporal plans with a start, an end and a duration per step, a critical-path total, and, through a composite task that lists each step twice, the earliest and latest possible time for that step. The site does not use any of that yet. Without a stated duration every step collapses to zero length, so the total reads as an instant: of 44 committed RFDs, 39 landed in the PR that created them, leaving a median lead time that is useless as a stand-in. - Add a composite window-rfd-N method to the generator that decomposes into earliest-rfd-N and latest-rfd-N, where the latest side needs its own again methods since the held shortcut no longer applies once the steps are already done (proposed). - Pair each step's two appearances in the navigator client as its earliest and latest possible time, with the problem document stating today as its origin (proposed). - Decide the declaration form for a duration, or a start and end per action, within the existing rebac block and with no new DSL (proposed). - Take the planner from the persona's latest release, as the navigator build already does, and check that tag carries temporal plans and the shortest-plan export (proposed). - Draft the 33 RFDs' durations from a reference-class estimate rather than the useless observed lead time, and report a range or a P50 or P80 finish instead of one critical-path total (proposed). Draft durations for the 33 RFDs in the cone, then run the navigator against the new temporal plan. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped. The blocker No RFD states a duration, and the observed lead times are not a usable stand-in: 39 of the 44 committed RFDs landed in the PR that created them, so the median lead time is 0 days. Left unfilled, every step in the generated domain is instantaneous and the plan's total reads as a zero-duration instant. The two generator changes scripts/pages_tree.exs needs a composite window-rfd-N method that decomposes into earliest-rfd-N and latest-rfd-N . The latest side cannot reuse the held shortcut, since by that point the steps it would shortcut are already done, so it needs its own "again" methods. site/navigator.js in the persona repository needs to pair each step's two appearances as its first possible and last possible time, and the problem document needs to state today as its origin , or every start and end point is left out. The planner release The navigator build ( site/build.sh in the persona repository) downloads the latest release tag of the persona repository, so no tag is pinned here. Whether that tag carries temporal plans and the shortest-plan export has not been checked against this work. Estimating durations The literature on duration estimates covers the planning fallacy, reference classes, three-point estimates, PERT merge bias, Monte Carlo methods and resource-constrained scheduling. These point toward a range or a P50 or P80 finish for the critical path, in place of one single total.

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the store's compaction moves off the write loop onto its own passive, timed thread. Scope: the store's fold and compact path in fdb_vfs.c, ported from a challenge submission. Can the store's compaction run on its own thread, on a timer, so a write caller never pays a fold's cost on its own latency? A winning entry in an outside challenge, rust-iouring-kensac, already runs its checkpoint and compaction off the write loop on a second, low-priority thread, so write callers never wait on it. The store's compaction today is demand-driven: a call to weft_compact_due blocks whichever caller happens to ask for it. That is exactly the kind of tail latency a day-long benchmark is built to catch, since it measures the slowest save a day reaches rather than a p99. - Add a dedicated, lower-priority compaction thread that opens its own FoundationDB connection and runs folds passively on a timer once the log grows past a threshold, instead of folding on demand inside the caller's path. - Change weft_compact_due from a blocking fold into a cheap call that wakes the thread when the log is already short, so the write loop never performs the fold itself. - Bound the hold time the compaction thread may take per pass, following the referenced entry's bound of at most 250 milliseconds, so passive compaction cannot itself become a tail-latency source. - Verify the change against the existing day-long benchmark that measures the slowest saves a day reaches, not only the median or the p99. Add a dedicated, nice'd compaction thread on its own FoundationDB connection, and measure whether a planted burst of writes still shows a fold cost on the write caller's own latency. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2460: Store: off-the-loop passive compaction thread (transfer from rust-iouring-kensac)

b: State: prediscussion Feature: hot store reads would skip SQLite's bytecode engine via direct B-tree cursor walks. Scope: the store's read paths over the weft_fdb VFS, with a SQL fallback kept. Does skipping SQLite's bytecode engine on the store's hot read paths buy a real win once the read side is already network-bound? The same outside challenge entry that inspired the compaction thread also walks SQLite's B-tree cursors directly inside a read transaction, skipping the SQL engine and its column copies, and decoding record bytes by hand with a SQL fallback kept for safety. The store's reads already go through prepare and step today. The honest read is that this is a constant-factor win, not a network round-trip win: the store's existing speculative reads and read-ahead already save roughly a round trip per read and turn two hundred fifty six pages into about two round trips, so the entry's trick can add at most something like five to fifteen percent, and only if profiling shows the SQL engine's overhead is real. - Profile the store's hot read paths before writing any cursor-reading code, to confirm whether the SQL engine's prepare and step overhead is actually a measurable share of read latency. - If profiling supports it, add a cursor-based reader that walks the B-tree directly inside a read transaction and decodes record bytes by hand, with the existing SQL path kept as a fallback rather than removed. - Treat any win here as a constant-factor improvement on top of the already network-bound read path, not a replacement for the speculative-read and read-ahead work already in place. - Do not spend further effort on this transfer unless the profiling step above actually shows engine overhead large enough to matter. Profile the hot read paths first; only build the cursor-based reader if profiling shows engine overhead worth the complexity, and keep the existing speculative read and read-ahead engineering untouched either way. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2461: Store: B-tree cursor reads on hot read paths (secondary transfer from rust-iouring-kensac)

b: State: prediscussion Feature: run-time i32 values become i32 tensors on the device instead of a refusal. Scope: the StableHLO lowering in guest/pjrt-rd/stablehlo.cpp and its generated test cases. Can an i32 value computed at run time reach the device, instead of being refused because it was not already known when the graph was compiled? Today an i32 value is folded away on the host whenever the compiler already knows it, and refused the moment it is computed at run time: an argument, or anything derived from one. Gather's index arithmetic and dynamic masks need those values on the device, not on the host, and the five graphs the probes run (qwen, dit, sconv and the two Kimodo layers) all touch one. Hold run-time i32 values as i32 tensors on the device, and add element-wise kernels under XLA's wrapping semantics: add, subtract, multiply, compare, select, clamp, and convert to and from f32. Lift each refusal that exists only for lack of one of these kernels, case by case, so that every case in the generator is either bit-equal on the GPU or carries a measured reason in XFAIL, with all 11 desk gates kept green throughout. Run the generated cases, including zeros of both signs, infinities, NaN and denormals, against XLA CPU's own output from the Zen 2 desk as the reference, and confirm a case built to fail does fail. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped. Cases and reference tools/gen_stablehlo_cases.py exercises the special values a run-time i32 path must survive: zeros of both signs, infinities, NaN and denormals. XLA CPU's own output, taken from the Zen 2 desk, is the bit-equal reference for every case; there is no other oracle in use here. What ships - Run-time i32 values held as i32 tensors on the device, never folded away because they were not known at compile time. - Element-wise kernels: add, subtract, multiply, compare, select, clamp, and conversion to and from f32, each under XLA's own wrapping semantics rather than a saturating one. - Refusals lifted only where one of the kernels above now covers the case; a case no kernel covers keeps its refusal unchanged. Acceptance - Every case in tools/gen_stablehlo_cases.py is bit-equal on the GPU, or carries a measured reason recorded in XFAIL. - A case built to fail does fail; a gate that cannot fail proves nothing. - All 11 desk gates still pass after the change lands.
t: RFD66606-2468: StableHLO: run-time i32 arithmetic

b: State: prediscussion Feature: reduce and dot_general reproduce XLA CPU's own order of summation, not only its sum. Scope: the StableHLO lowering in guest/pjrt-rd/stablehlo.cpp and its generated test cases. Can the lowering reproduce XLA CPU's own order of adding floats, not only the value that order happens to land on? Eight cases are not bit-equal on the RTX 4090 today: dot_batched, mlp_pre, mlp_f32, reduce_sum_random, mean_last, softmax_f32, rms_norm_f32 and causal_attention. Each stays within the functional bar, a rel-L2 around 1e-7 and at most a few dozen ulp, but none is bit-equal. reduce with add sums in an irregular tree that changes with the shape, and dot_general runs as a fusion whose accumulation tree also depends on the shape; cases with the order written out, or whose partial sums are exact, are already bit-equal, so the gap is the order, not the arithmetic. Reveal XLA's accumulation tree for each reduce and dot shape the five graphs use, on the Zen 2 desk with this jax build, and record the trees in a table keyed by shape. Emit each tree as a sequence of slices and adds, or as a kernel that takes the tree as data, and fall back to today's order, with the case kept in XFAIL, for any shape the table does not cover. The table is tied to one CPU and one XLA build, the way rsqrt_zen2 already is, so it records both. Reveal one new shape's tree, add it to the table, confirm that shape's case turns bit-equal, and confirm removing the table brings the old difference back. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped. The eight cases dot_batched, mlp_pre, mlp_f32, reduce_sum_random, mean_last, softmax_f32, rms_norm_f32 and causal_attention: each is within the functional bar today, a rel-L2 around 1e-7 and at most a few dozen ulp, but not bit-equal. pinned_sum_tree, softmax_pinned and causal_softmax_pinned already pin the order and are already bit-equal, which is the evidence that order, not arithmetic, is the whole gap. The two trees to reveal - reduce with add: an irregular summation tree that changes with the shape, matching an unrolled chain of adds reassociated by LLVM. tools/reveal_sum_order and the notes in STABLEHLO.md describe how it is read back out. - dot_general: a fusion whose accumulation tree also depends on the shape, revealed the same way, on the same desk and jax build. Acceptance - The eight cases above are bit-equal on the GPU, or each keeps a measured reason in XFAIL. - Removing the table brings back the old differences; that is the control this decision must fail without. - The added cost in dispatches and time for the five graphs is measured and written down. - All 11 desk gates still pass.
t: RFD66606-2469: StableHLO: match XLA CPU's summation order in reduce and dot_general

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the ported blocks-world GTN climbs from small instances to the five official ones. Scope: the blocks_gtn domain, its frontier harness, and the MiniZinc checker that grades it. Can a plan the GTN (goal-task network) finds for the Challenge's blocks-world also be the minimum, checked by the Challenge's own tool, climbing from the smallest instance up? GTPyhop's blocks_gtn is already ported, with take, put and moveblocks as a KHR_interactivity graph, and shortestOf already finds the optimal six actions for the Sussman anomaly. A separate reference tool already matched a breadth-first minimum for n = 3 to 7 on 3 piles, in times climbing from about 15 ms to about 4 s, but the domain still has no pile limit, no climbing harness and no run against the real checker. Encode the model's pile limit, k piles with at most k cubes on the table, in the GTN domain, then climb: generate instances at n = 3, 4, 5 and up with the model's k, record solve time at each step, and stop at the frontier where the time makes the next step not worth running yet. Add a heuristic lower bound, for instance the count of cubes already out of place, to prune the five official instances (16 cubes on 4 piles), which are far past what iterative deepening alone can reach. Validate every plan against MiniZinc itself, installed locally, rather than against the reference tool alone. Install MiniZinc, replay a solved instance through it, and confirm the checker accepts the plan as valid and minimum; a plan with one move removed must be refused by the same checker. Already in place - tests/gtpyhop/blocks_gtn/ ports GTPyhop's blocks_gtn: actions take, put and moveblocks as a KHR_interactivity (the Khronos node-graph behaviour format) graph. - shortestOf, iterative deepening over the backtracking decomposition and exported as persona_plan_shortest, finds the optimal six actions for the Sussman anomaly, and refuses a smaller bound by name as limit. - On branch parked/minizinc-blocks-frontier, tools/minizinc/ holds an instance generator, an independent breadth-first minimum, and a replay against the model's rules. For n = 3 to 7 on 3 piles, 20 random instances each matched the minimum and replayed validly, at a cost climbing from about 15 ms at n = 5 to about 4 s at n = 7. What still has to land - The model's pile limit, k piles and at most k cubes on the table, encoded in the GTN domain itself rather than assumed. - The climbing harness: generate n = 3, 4, 5 and up at the model's k, record solve time, and stop at the frontier; the stopping point teaches which bound or heuristic to add next. - A heuristic bound, such as a lower bound on cubes out of place, to prune the rising search enough to reach the five official instances, each 16 cubes on 4 piles. - MiniZinc itself, installed locally (brew install minizinc; there is no cask by that name, and minizincide is the IDE, not the checker) so a plan is validated for real, not only by the independent breadth-first tool. - A local clone of the MiniZinc/mzn-challenge archive, about 570 MB at depth 1, to read the 2022 blocks.mzn model this domain targets. Source MiniZinc/mzn-challenge, 2022/blocks-world/blocks.mzn: n cubes, at most k piles, minimise moves. Related - RFD66606-2339, where a persona answers from a goal-task network and exports a plan. - RFD66606-2292, the organization's own RECTGTN (Lean goal-task network) domain that renders this register. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2470: MiniZinc Challenge: blocks-world on the GTN blocks methods, climbing from small instances

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the temporal plan expresses the Challenge's precedence-only scheduling problems. Scope: the persona's temporal plan representation, read against four candidate problem sets. After the planning puzzles, can the same temporal plan express a problem that needs only precedence and durations, with no resources at all? Four problem families on the Challenge's list look like a fit by name alone: project-planning (2012, 2015), road_construction (2014, 2017), ship-schedule (2011, 2012, 2014) and train-scheduling (2024). None of their models has been read yet, so fit is a guess today. The temporal plan already carries start, end and duration per step, release times and deadlines, and a critical-path total, but it has no resources, so any model with a cumulative constraint is out of reach before a single model is read. Read each of the four candidate families' models, starting with the smallest, and classify each as expressible or out of reach by the same rule the planning puzzles used. For a family that is expressible, climb from its smallest instance, validate every plan against MiniZinc itself, and accept only a plan that is both valid and optimal. A family that needs a resource, an all-different, a cumulative or a packing constraint is set aside rather than forced onto a plan that cannot carry it. Read one family's model in full and classify it: expressible on the temporal plan as is, or out of reach because it needs a resource, an all-different, a cumulative or a packing constraint the plan does not carry. The candidate families - project-planning (2012, 2015) - road_construction (2014, 2017) - ship-schedule (2011, 2012, 2014) - train-scheduling (2024) None of their models has been read yet; whether each is expressible on the temporal plan is a guess from the name alone, not yet a finding. What the temporal plan already carries Start, end and duration per step (an unspecified start and end are left out of a problem; a missing duration means the step is instantaneous), release times and deadlines, and a critical-path total. It carries no resources, so a model with a cumulative constraint cannot be expressed on it as it stands. Acceptance The same rule the planning puzzles used: valid and optimal, checked against MiniZinc itself, climbing from the smallest instance of a family up, never starting at the largest. Source The problem list is at minizinc.org/challenge/globals/. b: State: prediscussion Feature: the Lean KHR_interactivity interpreter's gap against the extension's own text. Scope: Persona/Khr.lean, the Lean module that builds and runs a KHR_interactivity graph. Which of the extension's own nodes and types does the interpreter not build yet, and which checks does it only do while a graph runs rather than before it starts? Persona/Khr.lean already follows the extension's text for typed int and bool, 32-bit wrap, flow/for re-reading endIndex, socket order by string, variable/set with index-named sockets, pointer/get with isValid, and math/switch. Floats, float vectors, matrices and quaternions are not built at all, a float type simply rejects the graph, and a long list of nodes, reference template parameters and static type checking are missing too. A plan or a goal from elsewhere in this workspace can carry an unbounded integer; the extension's own integers are 32-bit two's complement, and that gap sits underneath every node listed here. Build the missing pieces in the order they block a real graph: first the float and float vector types (so a float type stops rejecting the whole graph), then flow/doN, multiGate, waitAll, throttle, setDelay and cancelDelay, then the remaining events beyond event/onStart, then variable/interpolate and pointer/interpolate, then the integer operations div, rem, sign, clamp, the shifts, clz, ctz and popcnt, then pointer/set's err flow, matrices and quaternions, and reference template parameters including the doubled-bracket escape for a literal bracket. Move every socket type check that runs today only while a node executes to a static pass before the run starts, so a mistyped graph is refused before any node fires. Build one missing node, give it a positive and a negative control, and confirm a graph that used to reject it now runs it, while a graph with the wrong socket type for it still refuses. Already built Typed int and bool, 32-bit wrap, flow/for re-reading endIndex, socket order by string, variable/set with index-named sockets, pointer/get with isValid, and math/switch, each following the extension's own text. Types not built Floats and float vectors, matrices and quaternions; a graph that declares a float type is rejected outright today rather than run. Nodes not built flow/doN, multiGate, waitAll, throttle, setDelay, cancelDelay; every event other than event/onStart; variable/interpolate and pointer/interpolate; the integer operations div, rem, sign, clamp, the shifts, clz, ctz and popcnt; and pointer/set's err flow. Syntax not built Reference template parameters written as {name}, and the doubled-bracket escape used for a literal bracket inside a pointer template. Checking that runs too late Every socket's type is checked only while a node runs, not before the run starts, so a mistyped graph can run partway before it is caught. The integer width gap underneath The planner's own integers, outside a KHR_interactivity graph, are unbounded. The extension's own integers are 32-bit two's complement. Every node above inherits this gap until it is closed once, at the boundary, rather than node by node. Related - RFD66606-2339, where a persona answers from a goal-task network and exports a plan as a KHR_interactivity graph. - RFD66606-2292, the organization's own RECTGTN (Lean goal-task network) domain this interpreter's planner side composes in. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the planner's backtracking search finds the shortest plan without an exhaustive scan. Scope: the planner's bound-raising search and the domains it solves. Can the planner find the shortest plan for 16 cubes without scanning every bound in turn? shortestOf raises a bound on the number of actions until a plan reaches its goals, through a backtracking decomposition. That search is exhaustive at each bound, so the whole search is exponential: fine for the Sussman anomaly at six actions, too slow for 16 cubes. Add three heuristics to the bound-raising search, each kept only if it holds plan length unchanged while cutting search time: - A lower bound supplied by the domain (admissible, so the rising bound starts higher and prunes branches that cannot reach a shorter plan). - Memoising failed (state, bound) pairs, so a branch already shown to fail at a bound is never re-explored at that bound. - Ordering alternatives by a heuristic, so the search tries the branch most likely to reach the goal first, before the branches it would otherwise explore in declaration order. Each heuristic ships behind its own control: a planted domain that breaks admissibility, a planted stale memo entry, and a planted heuristic that always ranks last, each of which must make its gate fail. Run the blocks-world domain at 16 cubes under a wall-clock budget. A plan that returns within budget, at the same length an exhaustive search would find, passes. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2473: Planner search: heuristics for the shortest plan

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the dead-on gate reads every painted marker in perfect conditions, with no exceptions. Scope: dead_on.py , texture_markers.py , and the placed-marker set they score. Does every marker we paint scan dead on, with the camera square on and nothing in the way? Today the gate fails: 276 of 280 visible markers read (98.57%) with the original ids, 278 of 280 (99.29%) with the ids moved. Camera 74 fails with two different ids at the same spot, so that is a position fault: a sharply tilted surface strip sits beside the marker. Ids 664, 703, 1973 and 1268 fail only at some positions, so those are pattern faults, not position faults. Drop every marker id that fails the dead-on gate (held in DROP_IDS ) and require a 100% read rate on the rest. A dropped id's slot stays a hole on the garment rather than being refilled by a neighbour, so the drop list is stable across renders. Camera 74's failure is tracked and fixed separately as a position fault, since it is a tilt problem in the surface strip, not a marker pattern problem, and fixing it is out of this gate's scope. Run the full pass over all 2,600 placed positions once it finishes rendering, and read the gate against that pass: 100% of the markers left after dropping the failing ids must read. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped. The two fault classes - Position fault: a marker's own pattern is fine, but where it sits (near a seam, a sharp fold, or a tilted strip) keeps the camera from reading it. Camera 74's dual-id read at one spot is this class. - Pattern fault: the marker's pattern itself does not read cleanly regardless of where it sits. Ids 664, 703, 1973 and 1268, which fail only at some positions and not others, land here once position is ruled out. Where the code lands dead_on.py scores each rendered position against the expected id, and texture_markers.py paints the marker set onto the garment texture before render. Both are referenced from pull requests V-Sekai-fire/interactor-taskweft-persona 6 and 7 against https://github.com/V-Sekai-fire/interactor-garment-proxy. Open The full 2,600-position pass was still rendering at the time of this draft. DROP_IDS is provisional until that pass completes and confirms no additional ids fail.
t: RFD66606-2474: Suit markers: dead-on gate must read every marker

b: State: prediscussion Feature: a tag bench and a frontier table pick tag family, marker size and detector settings. Scope: tag_bench.py , frontier_markers.py , and the detector variants they compare. Which tag family, marker size and detector settings give the fewest wrong reads at distance and tilt? The first bench run was invalid: the flat sheets rendered mirrored, so flipping the frame read 263 markers instead of the expected count, which gave 3,913 of 3,917 tags "broken" and failed the control outright. That bug is fixed in tag_bench.py . A per-tag blocklist is not a usable gate on its own, since it only reacts to tags that already failed; the frontier table has to decide tag family, marker size and detector settings up front instead. Ship the frontier table as the gate that selects tag family, marker size and detector settings, replacing any per-tag blocklist approach. Detector settings already show they matter at large marker scale: a window of 3 to 203 and a threshold constant of 3 recovered most of the unread markers at 220 px, and that setting becomes the frontier's starting point rather than a fixed default. Re-render the bench and build the frontier table: detector variants crossed with distance and tilt, each cell holding its wrong-read count, plus a flipped-frame control that must itself read as broken. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped. The mirrored-frame bug The flat sheets used to validate detector settings rendered mirrored left-to-right. Flipping the frame before detection recovered 263 readable markers that the un-flipped frame reported as unreadable, which inflated the broken-tag count to 3,913 of 3,917 and made the bench's own control pass for the wrong reason. tag_bench.py now flips consistently with the render path. Frontier axes - Tag family: which marker dictionary is painted. - Marker size: physical size in mm (and the derived pixel count at a given camera distance). - Detector settings: adaptive-threshold window size and threshold constant. - Distance and tilt: the two viewing conditions crossed against every other axis. - Flipped-frame control: every cell also runs mirrored, and must report broken, not readable. Code tag_bench.py and frontier_markers.py , both in https://github.com/V-Sekai-fire/interactor-garment-proxy. Open The re-render and the full frontier table were queued, not yet run, at the time of this draft.
t: RFD66606-2475: Suit markers: tag bench and the marker frontier (variants against input families)

b: State: prediscussion Feature: island charting raises marker yield per island above the current id-pool cap. Scope: island charting (xatlas or a custom charter) and the fold test that screens markers. Can an island hold more than 2,600 markers without widening past the id pool of 3,917 that the 6x6, distance-9-or-greater family provides? Run b places 2,600 markers, which is the id cap of that family, even though the pool itself has room for 3,917. Marker squares cover only 24.6% to 28.3% of island area, well under the 50% cap (markers sit only in white squares), so the limit today is island layout, not the id pool or the per-square area cap. Raise yield per island by changing how islands are charted, trying in order: an xatlas crease patch with a size window, a custom charter, and larger islands via maxChartArea and maxBoundaryLength . Screen candidate markers with a 3D fold test before placement: the largest normal deviation within 37 mm separates unread from read markers at a median of 76 degrees versus 31 degrees. Dropping every marker over 90 degrees keeps only 90.3% of markers, so the 90-degree cutoff alone is not the gate; it is a pre-filter ahead of the dead-on gate, since it would not have caught the camera 74 fault on its own. Re-chart islands with one of the candidate options and show more than 2,600 markers placed at the same read rate as run b, with no marker id reused twice on one garment. Related - RFD66606-2467, the dead-on gate that the fold-test pre-filter feeds markers into. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2476: Suit markers: raise yield per island toward 2310 without the id cap

b: State: prediscussion Feature: corners are placed by lattice voting, so markers read even when their id is wrong. Scope: predict_neighbours.py , the chart's lattice, and the corner-voting gates it must pass. Can a corner be placed on the chart correctly even when the id painted next to it is wrong? Treat the board as a spatially coded pattern instead of a set of independently-read tags: detect corners without trusting their ids, place each corner on the chart by voting over offsets, rotations and instances, and recover unread markers from their read neighbours. predict_neighbours.py already exists for this but was never run, and was left out of the earlier pull requests. Ship three gates ahead of any measurement, each with its own planted-defect control: - A planted wrong offset must lose the vote, so one bad candidate never outvotes the consistent majority. - A blank pattern (no corners detected) gives nothing back, rather than a false placement. - The UV pass marks every assignment right or wrong, with no assignment left unjudged. Once those three gates pass, measure corners placed, wrong placements, and markers recovered that tag decoding alone misses, and report those three numbers together, not separately. Run predict_neighbours.py against planted gates before trusting any measurement from it. Related - RFD66606-2467, the dead-on gate this recovery path feeds markers back into. - RFD66606-2469, island charting and the fold test that screens markers before placement. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2477: Suit markers: structured-light decoding with anonymous corners and lattice voting

Can ANNY-soma-x (the reference rig's SOMA-X variant) read a keypoint head, a hair occluder and a muscle-driven motion source without crossing a licence line? Nothing is started yet. RF-DETR Keypoint (Preview, 576 px, Apache-2.0) runs on the Windows desk, a pixi env with Python 3.12 and CUDA PyTorch; depth from it is ground truth only, never training data. HairDeck covers hair as both an occluder and an avatar part on CUDA. muscle-supermimic's MyoFullBody (24 GB) and the entities-model-explorer motion clips are the motion sources, retargeted to the 78 ANNY joints with rotation-star. The licences read on 2026-11-02: SOMA-X and ANNY code are Apache-2.0, ANNY data is CC0, so ANNY-soma-x meshes and datasets can be published with attribution; AMASS clips stay non-commercial and unpublished; HairDeck hair assets are unchecked. - Run RF-DETR Keypoint on the Windows desk's RTX 4090 pixi env (Python 3.12, CUDA PyTorch). Its depth output is ground truth for evaluation only and is never folded into training data. - Add HairDeck on CUDA for two roles: hair as an occluder in the keypoint pass, and hair as an avatar part on the published mesh. - Retarget muscle-supermimic's MyoFullBody (24 GB) and the entities-model-explorer motion clips to the 78 ANNY joints with rotation-star as the motion source for muscle-driven poses. - Clear each asset against its licence before publish: SOMA-X and ANNY code (Apache-2.0) and ANNY data (CC0) clear ANNY-soma-x meshes and datasets for publication with attribution. AMASS clips stay non-commercial and are never published. HairDeck hair assets stay unchecked until their licence is read, and are held out of any publish manifest until then. A keypoint head, a hair occluder pass and one retargeted muscle-driven clip each run end to end on the desk, and the publish manifest lists every asset's licence class. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped. The pose and shape sweep The sweep covers the pose and shape space ANNY-soma-x must cover: a grid of body shapes crossed with a set of muscle-driven poses from the retargeted motion clips, each rendered through the RF-DETR keypoint head with HairDeck's occluder active. Open questions - Whether rotation-star retargeting onto the 78 ANNY joints preserves muscle-supermimic's joint limits, or needs a clamp pass. - Whether HairDeck's licence, once read, permits the same publish path as SOMA-X and ANNY data, or restricts hair-bearing renders to an unpublished set. - Whether RF-DETR's 576 px input resolution undersamples the hand and face keypoints ANNY needs, or a crop-and-rerun pass is required.
t: RFD66606-2478: ANNY-soma-x: RF-DETR keypoints, HairDeck, muscle-supermimic and the pose and shape sweep

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the Maple dress fit's leftover hem, blendshape and weight issues get closed out. Scope: the Maple dress garment, its Unity scene and the body it fits in that scene. Does the Maple dress read clean in Unity once its cloth-fit (PolyFEM + IPC) pass is done, or do spikes, a stray blendshape and stale weights still show? The Maple fit left four items open: hem spikes on the dress, the ClothFit blendshape that the fit shipped back into the Unity scene instead of consuming, other outfit pieces that were not carried through the same fit, and scene body weights that still reflect the pre-fit body. The unity-garment-cloth-fit skill covers the fit and bind steps these items touch. - Smooth or re-solve the hem spikes left on the Maple dress's cloth-fit result until the hem reads flat in the Unity scene. - Remove the ClothFit blendshape the fit shipped back into the Unity scene; it is a solver artifact, not a scene asset, and must not ship on the mesh. - Carry every other outfit piece on the Maple body through the same cloth-fit pass the dress used, so no piece is fit to a stale body. - Rebind the scene's body weights to the fitted body so skinning matches the cloth-fit result, following the unity-garment-cloth-fit skill's bind step. The dress renders in Unity with no hem spikes, no ClothFit blendshape left on the mesh, every other outfit piece carried through the same fit, and body weights matching the fitted body. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the lone-writer baseline that every pair-matrix ratio divides by gets measured. Scope: the scratch FoundationDB cluster's contention benchmark and PROTOCOL.md. Why did the M=1 pair writer run about 142 commits/s at max rate, when a lone writer ran 90-114 commits/s in every other run? Every "ratio to M=1" in the pair matrix divides by the lone-writer baseline. The 0.68-0.73 bend seen at M=4 and M=8 may be mostly an inflated denominator: pairs at M=4 and M=8 ran 98-101 commits/s, the same as a lone writer. See the details for the logs behind both figures. A Mac power-state or clock effect is a hypothesis, untested. - Alternate the lone writer and the M=1 pair back to back, three cycles, on the same 4-process scratch cluster (never port 4700), same 15 s cell length, using mac/contention.c and mac/scratch-fdb.sh. Record load average, writer p50 and p99, and commits over 100 ms. - Fixed before the run: if the lone writer and the M=1 pair land within 10% of each other, call it no effect, and recompute every pair ratio against the lone-writer figure. - Fixed before the run: if they land outside 10%, name the cause before any ratio is quoted. Run a CPU-burner control, an idle-core spinner next to a lone writer, and require it to move the lone writer's rate; if it cannot, drop the power-state hypothesis. - Ship a table in the repo (min/mean/max over the cycles) and one line in PROTOCOL.md stating which baseline the pair ratios use. If the cause is not found, mark it undetermined rather than guessed. A table in the repo, built from the log files, giving min, mean and max commits/s for the lone writer and the M=1 pair across the alternating cycles, plus a one-line PROTOCOL.md amendment naming which baseline the pair ratios use. The logs behind both figures results-contention-matrix4.log (commit 1b6db4e) shows the M=1 pair writer at 141.8-142.0 commits/s across three repeats at max rate. Lone-writer runs on the same scratch cluster shape read lower: results-contention-matrix2.log gives 98.7-106.9 commits/s with stores=1; results-contention-matrix3.log (482974a) gives 89.7, 100.7 and 98.5 commits/s; and results-contention-matrix5.log (6be7ddb), a bare libfdb_c loop at N=1, gives 106.5-113.5 commits/s. The first matrix on a one-process cluster showed the same jump: 111 commits/s alone, 150 with 2 readers. Related - RFD66606-2474, the companion WSL-desk run that separates the Mac from the cluster. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2480: Settle the single-writer baseline: lone writer against the M=1 pair

Do the per-process bend (N=8 at 0.68-0.73 of N=1) and the 100-730 ms commit stalls belong to the scratch cluster's commit path, or to this Mac? results-contention-matrix5.log (6be7ddb), a bare libfdb_c loop with no SQLite and no VFS, gives per-process commits/s at N=1, 2, 4, 8 of 106.5-113.5, 89.3-112.9, 90.5-101.1 and 72.7-82.8; the ratio to N=1 at N=8 is 0.68-0.73. b: State: prediscussion Feature: the reader bend gets re-measured on a realistic feed-shaped table, not a toy one. Scope: the scratch FoundationDB cluster's VFS, its test table, and PROTOCOL.md's pair cells. Does the reader bend survive a realistic table? In the pair matrix, per-pair reads fell to 0.65-0.67 of M=1 at M=8 with the writer fixed at 50 commits/s, and to 0.47-0.48 with the writer at max rate. The current test table has 2,000 rows, about 500 KB, with a total store size probably around 4 MB, which data distribution almost certainly keeps in one shard on one storage process; adding storage processes would then change nothing, so a "not the cluster" conclusion drawn from it would be wrong. Under NORMAL locking, SQLite drops its whole page cache on every head move, so each uncached page costs one round trip when the speculative get hits and two when it misses, and a 500 KB table flatters that cost. Three candidate causes must stay separate: one storage process serving every page read, the VFS re-fetching pages after each head move, and this Mac. - Build a 50-200 MB table with the challenge's schema shape (schema.sql: users, posts, likes) and run a feed-shaped query against it. - Before reading any result, record cluster.data.partitions_count and the per-role query counters from status json, and read per-process CPU as deltas of cputime, never ps %cpu. - Repeat the M=1 and M=8 pair cells, three repeats, under the pre-registered reading rule in PROTOCOL.md. - Report a measured partitions count above one, or a stated reason it stayed at one, and the M=8 reader ratio with its confounds stated. - Any change to fdb_vfs.c goes on a dev/ branch of datasource-store with a probe that fails without it, and only after this question is answered. A measured partitions_count above one (or a stated reason it stayed at one), and the M=8 reader ratio on the feed-shaped table with its confounds stated. Related - RFD66606-2473, the single-writer baseline the pair ratios divide by. - RFD66606-2474, the companion WSL-desk run that separates the Mac from the cluster. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2482: Build a 50-200 MB feed-shaped table before any read or cluster-shape claim

b: State: prediscussion Feature: a benchmark measures how many rows one SQLite transaction must carry to keep a FoundationDB-backed store at the challenge's write rate. Scope: the 4-process scratch cluster's writer loop, its batch sizes, and the commit-rate table the run produces. How many requests must one SQLite transaction carry so a server on this store keeps up with the challenge's write rate? One SQLite transaction is one FoundationDB transaction, and a commit costs a median of about 8.4 ms, so a server that commits per request caps near 100 writes/s per store. A lone writer through the VFS (the SQLite-on-FoundationDB virtual file system) measured from 89.7 commits/s to 106.9 commits/s, and a bare libfdb_c loop with no SQLite and no VFS measured from 106.5 commits/s to 113.5 commits/s per process at N=1. The challenge's user model is derived, not measured on this server, at about 165 writes/s at 20,000 users and about 830 writes/s at 100,000 users; re-derive from bench/load.js before quoting. - Run the writer on the 4-process scratch cluster (never port 4700), through the VFS, at K = 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, three repeats, in closed-loop and fixed-arrival-rate modes, and record whether any batch's dirty pages crossed into the VFS's staging path (FoundationDB bounds one transaction to 10 MB and 5 s). - Build a table from the log files with min, mean and max over the repeats; report rows/s, per-row p99 acknowledge latency, commits over 100 ms, and conflicted delta; name the knee batch size and amend PROTOCOL.md with the chosen batch window and size. - Run the crash-check control: a planted variant that acknowledges before the commit must show higher throughput and then fail the check; kill -9 right after an acknowledgement must still find every acknowledged row in the store. Run a writer that carries K row-writes in one SQLite transaction, for K = 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, three repeats, in closed-loop and fixed-arrival-rate modes. K=1 must reproduce about 100 commits/s or the probe is wrong. Rows/s must grow close to linearly in K until commit latency rises; that point is the knee. Data so far - Lone writer through the VFS: from 89.7 commits/s to 106.9 commits/s ( results-contention-matrix2.log , results-contention-matrix3.log , commit 482974a). - Bare libfdb_c loop, no SQLite, no VFS: from 106.5 commits/s to 113.5 commits/s per process at N=1, median commit about 8.4 ms ( results-contention-matrix5.log , commit 6be7ddb). - Derived, not measured on this server: the user model does a like with probability 0.15 and a post with probability 0.02 per iteration of roughly 21 s of think time (think-time bands of 3 s to 7 s, 3 s to 8 s, and 5 s to 15 s). That is about 0.008 writes/s per user, so about 165 writes/s at 20,000 users and about 830 writes/s at 100,000. Re-derive from bench/load.js before quoting. - The C leader already group-commits; this store's writer must too. Reading rule, fixed before the run - K=1 must reproduce about 100 commits/s. If it does not, the probe is wrong. - Rows/s should grow close to linearly in K until commit latency rises. The knee is the batch size the server uses. - Report rows/s, per-row p99 acknowledge latency, commits over 100 ms, and conflicted delta. Controls that must be able to fail - A planted variant that acknowledges before the commit must show higher throughput and then fail the crash check. - Crash check: kill -9 the writer right after an acknowledgement and confirm every acknowledged row is in the store. An earlier measurement found a store that acknowledged before durable, and this is the failure that catches it. Acceptance A table built from the log files, with min, mean and max over the repeats; the knee named; and a one-line PROTOCOL.md amendment stating the batch window and size the benchmark server will use. Related - RFD66606-2382, the skateboard's manifest, which names datasource-store's SQLite VFS over FoundationDB as the store this benchmark measures. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2483: Find the group-commit knee: rows per SQLite transaction against commits and p99

b: State: prediscussion Feature: the challenge seed loads once into a SQLite-on-FoundationDB store through the VFS, with its row counts and content hashes checked against the seed file. Scope: the import path for seed/feed.db into one store, and the counts, hashes and integrity check that verify the import. Can the challenge seed be loaded once into a store through the VFS, and verified? The seed file seed/feed.db is 238 MB: 50,000 users, 500,000 posts, and 2,016,005 likes, with its schema fixed by schema.sql . This table is also the 50 MB to 200 MB table that a sibling measurement needs. The seed is in WAL mode, but the VFS (the SQLite-on-FoundationDB virtual file system) needs journal_mode=MEMORY and locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE , and a 4 KiB page size, so the import cannot simply reopen the seed file as-is. The VFS already stages a commit too large for one FoundationDB transaction, which bounds one transaction to 10 MB, so SQLite's backup API or VACUUM INTO through the VFS may do the job without hand-chunking. - Look first for an existing import path in datasource-store : prove_big_commit.c , sqlrun.c , weft_sql.c , tpcc.c , and fly/backup-fresh.sh ; try SQLite's backup API or VACUUM INTO through the VFS before hand-chunking with ATTACH and rowid-ranged INSERT ... SELECT sized well under 10 MB. - Import the seed once, not at server start, with journal_mode=MEMORY and locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE set and a 4 KiB page size; record which path ran. - Verify with row counts per table against the file seed, a per-table content hash over an ordered SELECT compared with the file seed (reusing the content sha256 that seed/make-seed.sh prints, if it exposes one), and PRAGMA integrity_check . - Run the control: drop 1,000 posts from the store after import and confirm the hash and the count both catch it; record import wall time, bytes in the store, and cluster.data.partitions_count afterwards. Row counts per table match the file seed, a per-table content hash over an ordered SELECT matches the file seed, and PRAGMA integrity_check passes. A planted control, 1,000 posts dropped from the store after import, must be caught by the hash and the count. Look first for an existing path Candidates in datasource-store : prove_big_commit.c , sqlrun.c , weft_sql.c , tpcc.c , fly/backup-fresh.sh . The VFS already stages a commit too large for one FoundationDB transaction (the 10 MB limit), so SQLite's backup API or VACUUM INTO through the VFS may do the job. Hand-chunk only if nothing exists. Method notes - The seed is in WAL mode. The VFS needs journal_mode=MEMORY and locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE , and the page size must be 4 KiB. - Import once, not at server start. - If hand-chunking: ATTACH the file seed and INSERT ... SELECT in rowid ranges sized well under 10 MB, or rely on staging, and record which path ran. Verification - Row counts per table against the file seed. - A per-table content hash over an ordered SELECT , compared with the file seed. Reuse the content sha256 that seed/make-seed.sh prints if it exposes one. - PRAGMA integrity_check . Control that must be able to fail A planted missing batch (drop 1,000 posts from the store after import) must be caught by the hash and the count. Record Import wall time, bytes in the store, cluster.data.partitions_count afterwards, and which path was taken. Acceptance Counts and hashes match, the planted control fails, the numbers are committed, and the sibling measurement that needs this table is told it now has a table to use. Related - RFD66606-2382, the skateboard's manifest, which names datasource-store's SQLite VFS over FoundationDB as the store this seed loads into. This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
t: RFD66606-2484: Load the challenge seed into a store once, verified by counts and hashes

b: State: prediscussion Feature: a probe isolates whether FoundationDB, macOS scheduling, or cluster-wide pauses produce the slow commits seen in every benchmark arm so far. Scope: a plain fsync probe, trace-event correlation and a RAM-disk cluster arm, run against the bare libfdb_c commit loop. What produces the commits from 100 ms to 730 ms seen in every benchmark arm so far? results-contention-matrix5.log (commit 6be7ddb) ran a bare libfdb_c loop with no SQLite and no VFS (the SQLite-on-FoundationDB virtual file system), so the VFS is not the cause. Slow-commit clusters (events within 0.25 s of each other) numbered 24 across 12 cells: 14 touched more than one process and 10 touched one, correcting an earlier report that every cluster touched more than one process. A lone process stalled in 2 of 3 repeats, so sharing alone does not explain the stalls. Server CPU stayed near half a core, ratekeeper reported limited_by=workload throughout, and the scratch trace logs held one SlowTask event in total and no disk-stall events. - Run a plain C loop of write plus fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) on the same volume as the scratch cluster, recording the maximum latency, both alone and alongside a commit loop; if it stalls the same way, FoundationDB is cleared as the cause. - Correlate the wall-clock start of every slow commit against fdbserver trace events and against production fdbmonitor log activity; sample fs_usage or iostat during the cells; run a RAM-disk cluster arm on the Mac and the desk arm from the sibling scheduling probe. - Run the two controls: SIGSTOP a scratch fdbserver for 300 ms and confirm the detector reports a multi-process cluster; run with no load and confirm no stalls are reported. - Keep the three candidates separate and untested until a control decides each: the scratch tlog's fsync sharing the Mac's SSD with the production cluster, macOS scheduling of client processes, and a cluster-wide pause. Do not cite the commit-proxy latency lines in status json per cell; they are cluster-wide windows, repeated across cells. A cause counts only if a control reproduces or suppresses the stall on demand; otherwise it stays undetermined, with what was ruled out, built from log files. Data so far results-contention-matrix5.log (6be7ddb), bare libfdb_c loop, no SQLite and no VFS, so the VFS is not the cause: - Slow-commit clusters (events within 0.25 s of each other): 24 in the 12 cells. 14 touched more than one process, 10 touched one. - N=1: 8 clusters, all single-process. N=2: 4, all multi. N=4: 3, all multi. N=8: 9, of which 7 multi and 2 single. - An earlier report said every cluster hit more than one process. That was wrong, and this table corrects it. - A lone process stalled in 2 of 3 repeats (5 and 4 commits over 100 ms), so sharing alone does not explain the stalls. - Server CPU stayed near half a core. Ratekeeper said limited_by=workload throughout. - The scratch trace logs held one SlowTask event in total and no disk-stall events. - The commit-proxy latency lines in status json are cluster-wide windows, repeated identically across cells. Do not cite them per cell. Candidates, kept separate and all untested 1. The scratch tlog's fsync sharing the Mac's SSD with the production cluster. 2. macOS scheduling of the client processes. 3. A pause across the cluster. Method - Cheap decisive probe: a plain C loop of write plus fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) on the same volume, recording the maximum latency, run alone and alongside a commit loop. If it stalls the same way, FoundationDB is cleared. - Correlate the wall-clock start of every slow commit with fdbserver trace events (trace format with timestamps) and with production fdbmonitor log activity. - Sample fs_usage or iostat during the cells. - A RAM-disk cluster arm on the Mac. - The desk arm from the sibling scheduling probe. Controls that must be able to fail - SIGSTOP a scratch fdbserver for 300 ms: the detector must report it as a multi-process cluster. - A run with no load must show no stalls. Reading rule, fixed before the run A cause counts only if a control reproduces or suppresses the stall on demand. Otherwise it stays "undetermined", with the list of what was ruled out. Acceptance One named cause, or an explicit "undetermined" with what was ruled out, built from log files.
